item.title: F1's Dutch GP red-flagged after monster Verstappen crash
item.description: Formula 1's Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort was red-flagged at the start of the second lap following a big shunt for local hero Max Verstappen
item.dc:creator: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded:
Formula 1's Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort was red-flagged at the start of the second lap following a big shunt for local hero Max Verstappen.

In what is the final Dutch GP for the time being, as Zandvoort relinquishes its place on the grid, Verstappen lost control of his RB22 navigating the final corner and went into the barriers, necessitating an immediate suspension of the race due to the amount of debris and the precarious position of the car.

Verstappen reported to his team immediately that he was not hurt in the incident.

Pre-race rain had left the track dampened but it had dried enough for all 22 drivers to favour slicks for the start.

But cars were kicking up a substantial amount of spray coming through the final two corners and Verstappen crashed hard out of seventh place - having had a bit of wheel-to-wheel contact with his stand-in team-mate Liam Lawson earlier in the lap.

There was also a huge spin coming through the same corner for Gabriel Bortoleto, but he avoided the barriers and thus was able to continue in his Audi.

Lando Norris was the race leader ahead of Kimi Antonelli at the time.

item.title: Gary Anderson: Ferrari's deceptive Zandvoort upgrade explained
item.description: Ferrari's Zandvoort upgrades might not look like much but when analysed as a package, Gary Anderson reckons the attention detail could pay dividends
item.dc:creator: Gary Anderson
item.content:encoded:
It’s all about the details in Formula 1.

Ferrari’s Zandvoort upgrade - bolted on from sprint qualifying onwards, likely because Ferrari doesn't have many spares and didn't want to risk damage in practice - might not look like much, but it is the finer details that we are talking about that optimise the overall performance. In effect, they cost very little, so they don’t break the budget as far as the all-important cost cap is concerned.

This small detail change in the bargeboard mounting system (highlighted in cyan) acts as a flow preparation device for the underfloor. So even though it doesn’t look like much, it could very well have a reasonable effect on the performance and consistency of the underfloor.

The reduction in height of the outer vertical turning vane (highlighted in green) again allows the lower section of the foot plate (highlighted in purple) to have more influence over the direction the flow is going to take at that point.

This should allow the lower horizontal vane to be more powerful, which should create a more powerful sealing system along the sides of the floor.

The positioning of the floor leading edge splitters will best optimise the flow coming off that repositioned bargeboard mounting (highlighted with the orange arrow).

The horizontal turning vane running across those splitters will also work in conjunction with that modified bargeboard mounting, optimising the airflow to the undersurface of the floor's leading edge.

This detail on the trailing edge of the diffuser is another way to help with the consistency of the underfloor.

Using the increase in the chord length of the beam wing (highlighted in green) in that central section will improve the performance of the central section of the diffuser.

Moving the larger central section of the vertical trailing edge trip (highlighted in cyan) outboard will improve the consistency of that outer section where the vertical wall meets the top section. This transition is always susceptible to separation problems.

Overall, these developments are more about aerodynamic consistency as opposed to out-and-out downforce. Consistency is what gives the driver confidence, allowing them to dig deeper into their talent without getting bitten by sudden unexpected snaps, especially on corner entry.

Just one additional thing I've spotted. All the teams do their best to monitor the front and rear tyre temperatures; this is critical to that one-off lap in qualifying, as it’s always difficult to get front tyre temperatures.

You can see in these two pictures above that Ferrari has been playing around with the infrared camera position (orange ellipse) to get the best reading.

The old picture has no camera; the new one is on the endplate foot, and the alternative is pictured below on the outer endplate surface.

This will be the best place for the least aerodynamic compromise, as it won’t influence the outwash generated by the turning vanes mounted on the endplate foot.

item.title: What Verstappen thinks strong stand-ins have exposed about F1
item.description: Are the very respectable stand-in performances of Liam Lawson and Yuki Tsunoda at the Dutch Grand Prix evidence that Formula 1 has become too easy in 2026?
item.dc:creator: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded:
Are the very respectable stand-in performances of Liam Lawson and Yuki Tsunoda at the Dutch Grand Prix evidence that Formula 1 has become too easy in 2026?

That’s certainly what four-time world champion Max Verstappen was hinting at after qualifying, where his stand-in Red Bull team-mate Lawson was just 0.115s slower than him.

Yuki Tsunoda, who replaced Lawson at Racing Bulls and hadn’t driven the 2026 cars with just a single day of simulator work aboard the VCARB-03 prior to this weekend, was just 0.102s off regular Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad in Q2.

Verstappen thinks this is evidence of how much easier it is to get to the limit of these cars in qualifying, given their unique energy demands have taken the emphasis away from swashbuckling, elbows-out one-lap efforts - much to the frustration of drivers like Verstappen and qualifying specialist Charles Leclerc.

“Especially in qualifying, I think it's a lot easier nowadays with these cars to find the limit, because you're also in quite a few places where you're a bit down on battery and everything becomes a bit easier to land,” Verstappen said when asked if Lawson and Tsunoda’s gaps were evidence drivers can make less of a difference this year.

“I think that demonstrated quite well this weekend compared to the previous cars. For me, that's not a surprise.

“You see it already the whole season; everyone is always within one tenth, two tenths.

“If you have a very bad qualifying, three tenths. It's always the margins are small.”

Lawson’s one-lap gap to Verstappen: Dutch GP

FP1: +0.536s
SQ1: -0.165s
SQ2: +0.374s
Q1: +0.102s
Q2: +0.427s
Q3: +0.115s

Lawson is very familiar with the 2026 Red Bull Ford power unit, as it’s powered his Racing Bulls all year, but he’d never driven the Red Bull RB22 prior to Zandvoort.

Take an average of the gap to Verstappen from his two Zandvoort qualifying sessions and you get 0.245s, very close to Isack Hadjar’s average gap to Verstappen in 2026 so far (0.232s), albeit over a much bigger sample size.

That Hadjar gap is considerably lower than any average Red Bull team-mate qualifying gap to Verstappen since Daniel Ricciardo was his team-mate in 2018.

But of course that’s not necessarily all down to the new rules. Hadjar has done a sterling job this year, so much so that Red Bull isn’t even considering its number two driver for the first time in years.

And Lawson’s put in a stellar season with Racing Bulls, so his performing better in the senior team than he did at the start of 2025 also makes sense.

But Verstappen raises an interesting hypothesis. The Race, namely Edd Straw’s weekly driver rankings, have certainly been complicated by it being harder to separate the performance of the driver and car this year and make definitive intra-team judgements.

Drivers like Oscar Piastri have also complained that “computers behaving or misbehaving” are also often deciding qualifying sessions, so there’s less power in the driver’s hands.

Looking more generally at the gaps between team-mates in 2026 versus 2025, the gap between team-mates in six of the 10 teams (discounting newcomer Cadillac) has gotten smaller since last year. The average 0.303s gap between Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll is the largest intra-team gap this year, compared to the largest of 2025, the 0.735s between Verstappen and Yuki Tsunoda at Red Bull.

Perhaps it is the case though that it’s harder for Verstappen to destroy his team-mates like before, given the next biggest 2025 gap was 0.453s (George Russell-Kimi Antonelli).

Although that data again has caveats, like Lewis Hamilton and Antonelli’s increased competitiveness versus difficult 2025s, that aren’t necessarily to do with it being easier to get to the limit of F1 cars in qualifying. Plus the fact only half a season’s complete so there's plenty of time for those gaps to close or widen.

Stella thinks it's more difficult

But all of that is not necessarily evidence that things are easier for drivers in F1 2026, according to McLaren team boss Andrea Stella.

“These cars are classified by both our drivers - I don't know about the others - as difficult cars to drive,” Stella said when The Race put the topic to him.

“Definitely last year we could see much less scatter between the two drivers. Here, when a driver is a bit on the back foot, then this can be a large amount.

“They are difficult cars to drive for several reasons. At the start of the season, it was in the corners and then in the straights. In the corners because of the low grip, much less downforce, smaller tyres, and in the straights because of the inconsistencies of the deployment, or the fact that you may have a sudden superclip before braking and now you've lost your braking reference, or sometimes the frustrating element that you go on power early in high speed and now you're losing deployment later.

“So there were several angles from which driving this year's car was more difficult. Those related to the power unit, I would say that the drivers and the engineers are now more familiar with, have become more familiar with, and they are sort of more ready to cope with that.

“Still, in the debriefing of this qualifying, drivers refer to elements of the power unit behaviour which affect the consistency of pushing at the limit. So this is not completely gone, but it's much less than the start of the season.

“But the reason associated [with] the corners and the grip is still there. Even if all teams have added downforce, it's very difficult for the drivers to predict what the problem is going to be in braking, or whether the car will snap or not in traction.

“With the previous generation of cars, there was much, much more load aerodynamically and much more grip from the tyres, and it was easier. While it was difficult for the drivers because everything was happening much faster, it was easier because normally you had kind of one thing to cope [with].

“Here, there's a lot that can happen at any moment from a grip consistency point of view, or even sensitivity to the wind, which in Hungary, or here, played a major part in the fact that nobody here had a clean lap in qualifying.”

Asked about Verstappen’s comments that F1 2026 put less onus on drivers’ skill, Stella replied: “I'm not so sure, like I'm genuinely not sure, and I would be inaccurate if I commented for another team.

“If I comment for what I've understood at McLaren, based on what I said before, I would say that this year is even more difficult.

“Like in the past, like in 2025, you needed to get used to the speed, and how fast things were happening. But this year you have to get used to adapt to the fact that you can have any kind of problem, because the car slides a lot.

“So it's, maybe this may depend on car characteristics, or even the driver's characteristics. But if I consider the McLaren experience, I think it's more difficult this year.”

item.title: Winners and losers from 2026 Dutch GP qualifying
item.description: Our winners and losers from Dutch GP qualifying at Zandvoort
item.dc:creator: The Race Team
item.content:encoded:
Our picks for the winners and losers from a highly competitive and close F1 qualifying session for the 2026 Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort.

Loser: Aston Martin Honda (18th and 19th) 

Progress from sprint qualifying, no doubt, but it was Lance Stroll’s verdict on Honda’s step forward that was most telling after qualifying. 

He called it a “small step” and said it’s “not nearly enough”.

Plus, it’s also created unwanted driveability issues that were first flagged in the Hungaroring filming day debut. It means the drivers are heading into corner entries uncertain of how much power they’ll have, and whether they’ll be fired off the road like Fernando Alonso was in SQ1 on Friday. 

“It's a lottery. Right now we're just not getting the consistent engine braking, going into the corner and a lot of rejected downshifts. So, yeah, a lot of issues,” was Stroll’s summary.

Those driveability issues need to be solved back at Honda HQ in Sakura, Japan, rather than trackside. So it’s unrealistic to expect improvements until Monza - where it could be even more punishing. 

Both drivers were effusive about the step with the chassis Aston Martin made in Hungary, but right now, according to the drivers, the spec 2 Honda hasn’t matched that. - Josh Suttill

Winner: Lando Norris (1st)

The reigning champion took his second-straight pole position and the second non-Mercedes pole position of 2026 - holding off both Mercedes drivers on Saturday afternoon in Zandvoort.

As the rain fell at the end of Q3, Norris held George Russell off as the Mercedes driver loomed in his wing mirrors, looking to overtake and gain clean air. That spot ahead of the Mercedes in Q3 proved pivotal to Norris’s pole lap.

“It doesn't get any better, a little surprised honestly. A decent lap, I was pushing as you've seen how close it is, every one-hundredth can make a difference,” he said. “A good turnaround from earlier where I felt we struggled a little bit."

This turnaround could prove crucial given that since Zandvoort returned in 2021, the Dutch Grand Prix has been won from pole position. - Samarth Kanal

Winner: Liam Lawson (8th)

Over five qualifying segments, Liam Lawson was an average of 0.128s off Max Verstappen at Zandvoort. Max Verstappen! It’s a result basically worth throwing a party for if you’re Lawson or one of his fans.

In two of those segments he beat Verstappen, and in the final one that counted, he was 0.115s off.

Verstappen’s almost impossible to beat. This Red Bull is so tough to drive. But still, Lawson has found a way to be relevant despite his lack of preparation stepping in for Isack Hadjar.

After how badly his first Red Bull stint went, you can understand why nobody is linking him with a permanent return to the works team. But that aside, he’s done about as well as you’d expect any driver to in these circumstances. - Jack Benyon

Loser: Ferrari (5th and 6th)

Ferrari’s qualifying hoodoo continues as the team just can’t get it going on Saturdays.

Hamilton and Leclerc are incredibly competitive on qualifying pace and were split by just 0.064s on Saturday afternoon - having been almost six-tenths apart in Friday’s sprint qualifying. But that’s really as positive as it gets. 

Leclerc explained that Ferrari made “mistakes in changing modes, power modes from Q2 to Q3. 

“That put me off a little bit with the feeling I had with the car and we'll have to look into it," he said. "But I don't think the potential for pole position was there anyway.”

Hamilton pointed towards poor tyre warm-up for his qualifying woes, but hopes Ferrari’s strong race pace can provide the consolation. 

With a solid start, the Scuderia could at least stay on the tail of the leading pack on Sunday - although the podium might be a stretch given how hard it is to overtake at Zandvoort. - SK

Loser: Pierre Gasly (11th)

There was a lot of hype about the upgraded Alpine of Pierre Gasly leading the midfield in sprint qualifying on Friday, but fast-forward to qualifying proper a day later and Gasly was left perplexed and out in Q2.

“If it was the absolute best lap and everything felt amazing and we're a tenth off, then it would be more concerning. I just think things didn't quite click yet,” was Gasly’s glass-half-full take on the situation.

Clearly the upgrades are a step forward, but Alpine hasn’t worked out exactly how to get the best out of them. That’s annoying as the sprint race showed how important qualifying is here, and the race will be tough tomorrow in terms of overtaking, at least to match Gasly’s P8 from the sprint race.

But he’s right ultimately that there’s no need to panic here. It’s just a case of inexperience with an upgrade package introduced early on one car only. - JB

Loser: Ollie Bearman (20th)

After being very critical of Haas’s car development on Thursday, Ollie Bearman followed that up with two Q1 exits behind his team-mate at Zandvoort, bagging 20th on Saturday, which was his worst result of the season so far.

“We did a few small changes [after the sprint], but there's not really much that we can do, to be honest with you,” Bearman said.

“We always end up running the same configuration, because it's the only way we can get any remnants of performance out of the car, and yeah, it's just not worked.”

Esteban Ocon pointed to the parts inconsistency issues affecting Bearman this weekend, which means "Every time you put a car down, you flip a coin and one car will work, one car will not".

This weekend, Bearman's isn't. - JB

Winner: Gabriel Bortoleto (9th) 

A huge slide at the exit of Turn 1 in Q1 nearly ended Bortoleto’s qualifying session early - yet he recovered, and then some.

“I don’t know what I’m doing,” he exclaimed on the radio after he took too much of the kerbs and had to reset.

The Brazilian driver recovered to 10th in Q1 and then went three-tenths faster than team-mate Nico Hulkenberg in Q2. 

He conceded it was a “scary moment” - and he almost repeated it in the following sessions - attributing his Q1 moment to the gusts around Zandvoort.

The Audi driver also outqualified Racing Bulls’s Arvid Lindblad (P10) and the upgraded Alpine of Gasly (P11).

Having missed out on a point in the sprint, Bortoleto now has a chance to score points for the third time in four weekends. - SK

item.title: 'Not nearly enough' - Stroll's verdict on Honda's F1 engine upgrade
item.description: Lance Stroll believes Honda’s upgraded Formula 1 engine is “not nearly enough” after Aston Martin’s double Q1 exit at the Dutch Grand Prix
item.dc:creator: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded:
Lance Stroll believes Honda’s upgraded Formula 1 engine is “not nearly enough” of a step forward after Aston Martin’s double Q1 elimination at the Dutch Grand Prix.

Aston Martin lost both cars in the first stage of sprint qualifying on Friday, but hopes were higher given that it was the first proper day of the new Honda engine running on a race weekend - plus the caveat of Fernando Alonso’s straight mode not working on his rear wing in sprint qualifying. 

And while the pace was better after the first runs, with Alonso 12th, ultimately both Aston Martin drivers fell short of a Q2 place, with Alonso a tenth adrift. 

Stroll was a tenth and a half behind Alonso and delivered a somewhat bleak verdict on Honda’s “small step” forward when quizzed about it after qualifying. 

“Not so much, I think. Maybe a bit, but not nearly enough,” Stroll said, when asked by The Race if he could feel a step forward. 

“On the chassis side, I think we're quite good. We made a big step in Budapest. The driveability and the power is the next thing we need to really work on.” 

He said there are “still a lot of issues on the engine side”, namely the driveability problems, which is making the Aston Martin very unpredictable on corner entries.

“Not good, not good. It's a lottery,” Stroll said of the driveability. “Right now, we're just not getting the consistent engine braking, going into the corner and a lot of rejected downshifts. So, yeah, a lot of issues.” 

Alonso: Aston Martin has taken "amazing" step 

Alonso felt like there was around a tenth more on the table with a better outlap for his final run, which wasn’t an improvement on his previous best.

But he was far from disappointed when comparing the much-reduced gap between Aston Martin and the ultimate Q1 pace of Oscar Piastri's McLaren.

“Piastri P1 in Q1 was 1.3 seconds in front of us - we used to be 4.5 seconds average on the gap to the leader, so we improved three seconds in two races," Alonso explained.

"This is amazing. Everything is working as expected, but this is a tough sport. You need to always keep improving.” 

He agreed with Stroll that there’s more time to be found if Honda can improve the driveability of the new power unit, but that can only be done at Honda’s Sakura base in Japan. 

“Unfortunately, here on the track side, there is not much we can do," Alonso added. "We need to rely on some big changes in the factory or software or whatever is needed.

"This has to come from Japan, so it's not from one day to the next. It's more towards Monza where we need to find another step there. There are a couple of tenths to optimise in the package.” 

As for Aston Martin’s prospects for the race from 18th and 19th on the grid, Alonso said: “Let's see. Normally we are doing better on the race pace because our chassis is very good. 

“When [rivals] have old tyres or older tyres in the race, we rely more on our good grip from the chassis and we don't rely so much on the tyres and grip.

"We can do a better job, but at the same time we cannot overtake on the straights. We are in a difficult position there, but we try our best.”

Honda's trackside general manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara said: “Today we ran the sprint race and qualifying without any reliability issues with the new spec engine.

"We have received similar feedback from both Aston Martin drivers after these sessions.

"Together, with our engineers’ assessments, and our work on the test bench at HRC Sakura overnight and after the sprint race, we have seen some improvements to get a better control over the internal combustion engine (ICE) and to further improve the consistency of the combustion behaviour in qualifying.

"We need to ensure that the engine does what the driver needs at the right time. We have taken some steps today, but there is still more to be done to give the drivers the confidence they need.

"This is our primary focus for the short and medium term.”

item.title: Norris takes pole in tense Dutch GP qualifying finale
item.description: Lando Norris made it back-to-back pole positions by topping qualifying at Formula 1’s Dutch Grand Prix, beating the Mercedes duo as rain loomed
item.dc:creator: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded:
Lando Norris made it back-to-back pole positions by topping qualifying at Formula 1’s Dutch Grand Prix, beating the Mercedes duo.

Norris took pole at Zandvoort with a 1m11.163s in Q3 to best sprint race winner Russell by just over a tenth of a second.

Norris and Russell were among those to set their final Q3 laps relatively in anticipation of rain at the end end of the session, with the McLaren driver ending up quickest.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli was third fastest, just 0.031s shy of Russell, with Oscar Piastri fourth, a tenth and a half adrift of his McLaren team-mate.

Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc set their final laps slightly later but ended up fifth and sixth with Hamilton the last of the leading teams to set a time, jumping Leclerc in the process.

Max Verstappen was seventh for Red Bull with his stand-in team-mate Liam Lawson doing a solid job to qualify eighth, just over a tenth slower.

Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto led the midfield fight in ninth ahead of Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls.

Having been the top midfielder in sprint qualifying and the sprint race, Pierre Gasly struggled in the upgraded Alpine, missing out of Q3 and ended up 11th.

Racing Bulls stand-in Yuki Tsunoda was 12th ahead of Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi and Franco Colapinto in the older spec Alpine.

Albon Albon made it back-to-back intra-team qualifying victories, beating team-mate Carlos Sainz by 0.022s to advance into Q2 while Sainz was knocked out in 17th place.

Albon ended up 16th as the slowest driver in Q2, half a tenth behind Esteban Ocon’s Haas.

Upgraded Aston Martin Honda falls short of Q2

The upgraded Honda engine went better in the back of the Aston Martins than it did in sprint qualifying, with Fernando Alonso 12th ahead of the final runs in Q1.

However Alonso couldn’t improve on his final lap and ended up being eliminated in 18th place, just ahead of team-mate Lance Stroll.

Ollie Bearman’s Haas was 20th - his worst qualifying of the year - ahead of the two Cadillacs, led by Valtteri Bottas for the fifth consecutive qualifying session.

item.title: Winners and losers from F1's Dutch GP sprint race
item.description: Formula 1's first (and last) ever sprint race at the Dutch Grand Prix was hardly a classic, but it did produce some winners and losers
item.dc:creator: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded:
Formula 1's first (and last) ever sprint race at the Dutch Grand Prix was hardly a classic, but it did produce some winners and losers.

Here's our team's picks...

Loser: F1

We’re going to have more sprint races in 2027, and while it wouldn’t be fair to judge that decision based purely on this turgid Zandvoort race, it’s at least a warning that F1 has to be very careful in choosing which races get the sprint treatment.

I’ve seen more action in supercar parades than this so-called 'race'. Up front, Leclerc’s dive down the inside of Lando Norris was the only overtake not assisted by the start, in which Kimi Antonelli jumped Oscar Piastri. Franco Colapinto also mugged Yuki Tsunoda at the start for 12th.

The retiring Audi of Nico Hulkenberg and Sergio Perez’s ailing Cadillac even assisted some of the rises up the order further down, too.

An awful race and I only hope qualifying and the race is better to give Zandvoort a more fitting F1 send-off as it leaves the calendar. Because based on that sprint, I’m happy it’s leaving, and that’s really not fair and very sad. - Jack Benyon

Winner: Charles Leclerc (2nd)

Thank goodness for Charles Leclerc’s gamble to wear soft tyres for the Zandvoort sprint, and to have the audacity to…make an overtake! Shocking.

It was a strong move on Norris in the second half of the race, although Leclerc reckoned it was boosted because he could see Norris didn’t have as much deployment on the straight as he did. Perhaps that will be a theme that runs through this weekend in terms of deployment styles and execution.

Using the soft tyres should have produced a gain at the start and a loss as they degraded at the end, but it looked the opposite for Leclerc, and he felt he and the team were vindicated by the “homework” they did on the softs.

Ultimately, he had a bad start which hampered early progress, but Leclerc and the Ferrari kept the softs in better condition for longer than some of the medium runners, which is an intriguing prospect for race day. - JB

Loser: McLaren (3rd & 5th)

Lando Norris’s rear tyres appeared to fall off a cliff just over a third of the way into this sprint race, and Oscar Piastri’s total anonymity in fifth just showed McLaren didn’t quite have the pace today.

Both drivers were victims of the only two meaningful overtakes of the race, respectively.

Hopefully they have learned a lesson from this that they can apply to the race as struggling that quickly on the mediums might make Sunday difficult for them if that continues. - JB

Winner: George Russell (1st)

Whatever George Russell did over the summer (and maybe it was his engagement), he has returned from the summer break refreshed and with exactly the mental approach needed to grab the results that keep his title hopes alive.

His Zandvoort sprint pole and victory (the third time out of five he has done the double this year) were helped by perfect execution in qualifying and some clever tyre management in the race – showing he is back at one with the W17.

The points deficit to Kimi Antonelli is still big (56), and he is going to need a bit of luck on his side, but Russell has shown he is far down and out from a first half to the campaign that did not go to plan. - Jon Noble

Loser: Liam Lawson (11th)

This placement isn't much of a reflection of Liam Lawson's driving in the Dutch Grand Prix sprint race, as he couldn't do much once Arvid Lindblad fended off his attack on the opening lap.

Thereafter, it was a frustrating race for Lawson, who couldn't make any impression on his usual team-mate.

Ultimately, Lawson was doomed by not making it into SQ3 on Friday and breaking into the top 10 will be the key goal for grand prix qualifying to ensure he doesn't get stuck again on Sunday of what's been a 'very respectable' stand-in weekend so far. But he'll need to do more than this to tip it into 'spectacular' territory. - Josh Suttill

Winner: Pierre Gasly (8th)

As with most drivers on the grid, this result was born out of qualifying, where the upgraded Alpine of Gasly led the midfield, and maintained that during the race.

Given the lack of overtaking, you wouldn’t want to read too much into this race. But despite early pressure, Gasly was able to gap Gabriel Bortoleto to the tune of nearly two seconds by the end.

Positive signs for a team which has felt in no-man’s-land while Racing Bulls’ upgrades had shoved it ahead in the pecking order. - JB

Loser: Nico Hulkenberg (NC)

With just seven laps completed in the sprint thanks to a "power issue right from the beginning", Nico Hulkenberg is the biggest loser in mileage terms.

He was always unlikely to score points from 14th on the grid, but he did need laps to understand his baffling SQ2 exit on Friday, which he had very few answers to explain. - JS

item.title: Russell wins static Dutch Grand Prix sprint race
item.description: George Russell won an uneventful Dutch Grand Prix sprint race
item.dc:creator: Jack Benyon
item.content:encoded:
Formula 1's 2026 Zandvoort sprint race could have been mistaken for a car parade rather than an actual race, as George Russell won from pole and only two changes of position happened in the top 10 over the 24 laps.

Lando Norris managed to keep Russell under pressure for the first stretch of the race but over laps nine and 10 he lost over a second to Russell with a tail-happy rear-end. That allowed Russell the breathing room he needed.

The only uncertainty was late rain, which hit almost immediately after Russell crossed the line. The perfect start for his bid to turn around his tough first part of the season.

The change of position in the top 10 at the start came when Kimi Antonelli jumped Oscar Piastri’s McLaren and set about chasing Charles Leclerc for the last spot on the podium.

As if doing the fans a favour by anticipating the turgid race, Leclerc added a grain of interest by bolting on soft tyres - alongside only 17th-place starter Ollie Bearman - which theoretically gave him a chance at making up early positions before degrading later on.

But with Norris ahead struggling a third of the way through with a loose rear, Leclerc was able to pressure him and on lap 18 he dived to the inside at Turn 1, pushing Norris wide and barging through for the only meaningful overtake of the race not happening at the start.

Leclerc wasn't able to catch Russell but avoided his softs going off dramatically at the end to seal second.

Norris immediately came under pressure from Antonelli once Leclerc went through, and Antonelli tried all the way up until the last lap when he half-tried a Turn 1 dive, but couldn’t make it stick and had to settle for fourth.

Piastri was a very distant fifth, dropped by Antonelli, while an intriguing battle between Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton - a regular occurrence in 2026 F1.

Hamilton dropped as far as two seconds behind at mid-race, having been close early on, but Hamilton closed back in during the closing stages, typically of this race, unable to make a move stick.

Pierre Gasly was under pressure for the entire race, but his upgraded Alpine yielded the final point for eighth ahead of Gabriel Bortoleto’s Audi.

Arvid Lindblad claimed another scalp as the Racing Bulls driver beat his usual team-mate Liam Lawson, who’s standing in for Isack Hadjar this weekend at Red Bull.

But before you condemn Lawson, remember the difficulty in overtaking in this race.

Yuki Tsunoda lost out to Franco Colapinto at the start, perhaps that could be put down to Tsunoda doing his first-ever race start with the complicated process required for 2026 cars.

So Colapinto - without the Alpine upgrade - took 12th ahead of Tsunoda.

item.title: The warning for Mercedes in its Zandvoort data
item.description: Though Mercedes is on Zandvoort sprint pole, the performance profile suggests a key McLaren gain
item.dc:creator: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded:
George Russell's sprint pole position at Formula 1's Dutch Grand Prix provided relief for Mercedes that its strategy of holding fire on upgrades had not yet dropped it into the pack.

While Ferrari and McLaren have been aggressive in bringing development packages to their cars – with latest updates from both appearing at Zandvoort – Mercedes has been playing the long game.

Having selectively had just one major spec change at the Canadian GP in May, it is saving its development spending for an end of season splurge when it hopes the coffers of its rivals are empty.

But despite Russell's form in edging out Lando Norris's McLaren showing that the W17 is still very strong, tucked away in the data is a clear warning signal that Mercedes may not be able to wait much longer before needing to bring more.

Russell's advantage over Norris to take pole was a slim 0.041 seconds, but there was a very topsy turvy nature to how they achieved their laps – with big variability between sectors.

                        SECTOR 1      SECTOR 2      SECTOR 3
RUSSELL        24.381s           25.434s      21.752s
NORRIS         24.622s           24.983s      22.003s

There was nearly half a second of difference between them in the middle sector, with Kimi Antonelli similarly adrift to show that this was a Mercedes trend. 

Under F1's 2026 rules, such variability is not uncommon and often comes from different deployment strategies – where one driver will use more energy on one straight compared to another.

Some of the difference between Norris and Russell can be explained from this, with there being a big speed difference for example as they run to end the lap.

As Russell's Mercedes keeps accelerating to 317km/h (197mph) in the chase to the timing line, Norris's McLaren peaks at around 307km/h (191mph) before falling away.

But the Mercedes advantage here does not seem to be the upside to it having deliberately not used energy elsewhere, as the only real difference in top speeds between them is when McLaren appeared to have used more at the start of the lap.

In fact, digging into the telemetry of their best SQ3 efforts, the poor middle sector of Russell's was nothing to do with saving energy on the straights – it was performance through the corners.

As the data above shows, which we have used from F1tel.com shows, Mercedes has been struggling compared to McLaren and Ferrari in the high-speed Turns 7 and 8 – which neither Russell nor Kimi Antonelli can take anywhere near as fast as McLaren and Ferrari.

While McLaren's upgrade has helped Norris keep his minimum speed up at 253km/h (157mph) through Turn 7 and 219km/h (136mph) at Turn 8, Russell drops to 242km/h (150mph) and 205km/h (127mph). 

Those differences pull Norris back from two tenths of a second adrift at the time, to back on par with Russell.

The performance through these two high-speed corners points to McLaren having made a clear step with its most recent upgrade – as it is in contrast to what we have seen in turns with such a speed range earlier in the year.

At Silverstone, for example, Norris was 7km/h (4.3mph) slower than Russell through Copse (283km/h vs 276km/h), and a similar speed adrift at Stowe (238km/h vs 231km/h).

What Mercedes now needs to understand is whether that speed offset through Turns 7/8 at Zandvoort is a sign that it has genuinely fallen back in high-speed corners so needs to respond with some car improvements, or if there is some set-up or driving approach issue that has left it exposed.

A clearer answer for that will come when Mercedes has another go at qualifying on Saturday afternoon.

item.title: Could have been 2.5s quicker?! Honda's deceptive F1 engine upgrade debut
item.description: The debut of Honda’s upgraded spec 2 Formula 1 engine proved to be a disappointment in sprint qualifying at the Dutch Grand Prix on paper
item.dc:creator: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded:
The debut of Honda’s upgraded spec 2 Formula 1 engine proved to be a disappointment in sprint qualifying at the Dutch Grand Prix on paper.

Aston Martin duo Lance Stroll and Fernando Alonso failed to make it out of SQ1 at the Dutch Grand Prix as the squad appeared to have made a step back from its promising Hungaroring weekend.

Stroll, who ended up 19th and six-tenths off making it to SQ2, was left struggling for answers about where he could have got more time from.

Alonso, who was 22nd and last after a first effort ended up with a big lock-up into Turn 1, suggested on team radio afterwards that Honda’s early-season vibration bugbear had returned.

“Huge vibrations on the straights,” he said. “And not from the tyres, eh....”

So, had Honda’s much-hyped, more powerful spec 2 engine fallen flat at the first hurdle? 

Not totally, but equally it has exposed that the improved power does not automatically translate to better laps yet.

The rear wing issue

Alonso's poor showing was quickly explained as not being down to a power unit problem.

Instead, it emerged – even though Alonso had not noticed it at the time – that his rear wing active aero had failed.

It meant that running down the straights, his rear wing had stayed closed in corner mode, which increased drag to reduce top speed. It also meant he burned through his battery pack quicker.

The end result was a 20km/h speed deficit compared to his best lap from practice into Turn 1 – and he was 2.3 seconds slower by the time he hit the apex.

A further two tenths were lost on the run between Turn 10 and 11, where he was 15km/h slower.

While it is not an exact science, if we take 2.5 seconds off Alonso’s laptime then he would have ended up in the mid 1m13.5s – which would have been easily enough to get through to SQ2.

But this comes with a caveat that team-mate Stroll did not have an SM problem and also did not make it out of Q1.

The SM issue had another impact on Alonso too, in that it pushed the car down more.

So, the ‘vibration’ experience that Alonso complained about on the radio may have been the result of the car grounding out and struggling as its rear got more loaded.

Sources suggest there had been no vibration issues during opening practice for Honda.

What does need sorting

While the reality of Honda’s showing did not match the laptimes delivered, it would be wrong to suggest that without the SM problem it would have been mission accomplished for Alonso, Honda and Aston Martin in continuing its push forward.

Both practice and qualifying had highlighted that there is still a mountain for Honda to climb when it comes to sorting out the driveability of the power unit.

The 2026 rules demand perfect performance under both acceleration and braking – with that corner entry phase particularly critical to maximising energy harvesting.

And this is an area where Honda has not yet got sorted with its spec 2 engine.

Alonso talked about the car pushing on as he slowed for turns, and it was this exact issue that triggered Alonso’s lock-up in SQ1 that derailed his first effort.

“When you brake and the throttle is open, it's difficult to stop the car,” he said.

Solving this requires a lot of detailed software tweaking and can take time - but that work was already starting in Japan on Friday night as Zandvoort closed up for the evening.

As Honda’s chief engineer Shintaro Orihara said on Friday night: “HRC Sakura will analyse the data overnight and perform dyno tests to optimise these parameters for the rest of the weekend.”

Having taken stock of things after getting out of the car, Alonso was certainly not as despondent about where things were with the spec 2 engine as he had seemed in the car.

“Free practice felt okay and I felt a step forward, I think it's very early days and probably a little bit immature, a little bit of the controls,” he said.

“It's a sprint weekend. On a normal weekend we had three practices to nail the package.”

Aston Martin and Honda will have another opportunity to nail it on Saturday afternoon, and hope to prove that the sprint qualifying showing was an anomaly rather than a sign that this is what their genuine performance is like.

item.title: Lawson's first day back at Red Bull was very revealing
item.description: Liam Lawson's 'second start' at Red Bull looks absolutely nothing like his first
item.dc:creator: Edd Straw
item.content:encoded:
For Liam Lawson to be frustrated after lapping a respectable 0.365s off team-mate Max Verstappen in sprint qualifying for the Dutch Grand Prix is revealing.

With just one free practice and a day in the simulator under his belt, Lawson looks significantly more comfortable with the Red Bull than he did at any point in his troubled two-event stint with the Formula 1 team last year - but even a margin well under half the deficit of the best of his three qualifying outings alongside Verstappen last year didn't do his underlying pace justice.

Lawson's elimination in SQ2, leaving him 11th on the grid for tomorrow’s sprint race, was so disappointing given it was out of kilter with what came before. He made that clear over the radio after the second of his two quick laps in that session, saying “I’ve no idea what happened in Q2”. He didn't have a clearer explanation after he got out of the car.

“Honestly, I don’t really know,” said Lawson of what went wrong in SQ2. “It's been an interesting day, but normally you'd improve through quali and we started SQ1 quite strong and then we didn't make the same step that everybody else did. Obviously we'll look into it, there's a lot to learn today, but so far I feel quite good in the car. I was honestly feeling OK through quali, I thought we'd get through, so it's a shame.”

Feeling “OK” in the car is what matters. You could see he was relatively at ease watching trackside in free practice at the banked Turn 3. Yes, he was a little more conservative than team-mate Max Verstappen in how he attacked the corner, as you would expect, but Lawson at least looked like he was on top of the machinery.

The main concern was that two of his quick laps at the end of the session resulted in him running wide and dragging the floor of the car across the exit kerb.

The last time I watched him in a Red Bull up close was in China last year, where he looked all at sea on what proved to be his final outing - until now - for the team. There, he was tentative, taking a trip through the gravel on his first push lap and never getting to grips with it, but here he looked nothing like that. He was not at Verstappen’s level today, inevitably, but in the circumstances it was a good start.

The same applies to SQ1. The first of his three push laps was slow, but that was down to traffic on the lap. His final two efforts were much more convincing, allowing him to end the first segment of qualifying 0.165s ahead of Verstappen in sixth place.

This raised expectations for SQ2, as even on a day when Red Bull was struggling Lawson appeared to have the pace to make the top 10. So to miss out, and only be a few thousandths ahead of the man who took over his usual car, Yuki Tsunoda, was understandably a blow.

Moving with the evolving track is one of the skills of qualifying, but it’s excusable not to have mastery of it for a driver who is unfamiliar with the car. There was a reminder of that at the end of SQ1, when he returned to the garage and referenced what Racing Bulls normally does with the front wing flap angle. He reported he was happy with the balance, and it’s not clear what direction Red Bull went in because the radio feed fell silent to the outside world, but understanding how a car might react to adding in a little more front wing as the track grip improves is something that comes with experience of the machinery. Given Lawson lacks that, the way today played out bodes well for the rest of the weekend.

“It definitely does,” said Lawson. “We'll obviously try and fix it and put it together for quali. But we definitely had the potential to be right up there today, so it's frustrating.”

What matters is that this was, all things considered, a good start for Lawson. And that's much better than what happened last year.
